items_missed: No agenda statement of any kind — no roadmap, no timeframe, no 'sound good?' confirmation.
Never used the customer's name once in a 6.9-minute call, even though he had her account pulled up ('I did pull up all of that information').

Let the customer audit her own move scope. She twice said 'I forgot the kitchen and the garage' — the rep never walked rooms, only asked one open question: 'would there be anything kind of outside of what's in these photos?'
Box count left completely unclarified. Customer said 'maybe like six' bins and a garbled box number, and the rep is building a fresh estimate on top of that without pinning it down.

Piano ignored. Customer said 'the biggest heavy things are probably gonna be and the piano' and the rep answered 'Okay, perfect. Perfect.' — no specialty-item handling, no crew/time implication, no damage-coverage mention.
No specialty/variable probing at all: no stairs, no walk distance, no access/parking, no additional stops, no storage, no packing needs.
Zero differentiators: no No Worries Damage Coverage, no Meet Your Mover, no On-Time Guarantee, no 'no hidden fees' pitch.
No typical time range for the job, and no equivalents framing even after the garage and kitchen were added to scope.
No assembly/disassembly mention despite a kitchen table and a treadmill being named.
Entire Save Your Ass prep speech missing on the single best possible setup — the customer was already self-consolidating ('my husband's gonna take that') and a next-day move was on the table.

No booking attempt. Tomorrow's 8:30-9:00 AM slot was live and the customer was interested ('I'm supposed to get the keys tomorrow'), and the rep still ended on 'we can kind of reconnect' instead of holding the slot.

Availability was checked only because the customer asked — and the check revealed both her preferred days had booked out overnight. The rep should have raised the booking-out risk proactively rather than being caught by it.
No 'no deposit required' mention — the exact reassurance that would have made holding tomorrow's slot easy to say yes to.

Never said the word 'email.' He offered to 'shoot you over an updated estimate' and the customer left the call expecting a phone callback ('I'll just wait for your callback') — channel confusion left uncorrected, no bolded-details recap, no 'reply with any corrections.'
No hours or how-to-reach-us before hanging up.
No clock mechanics (2.5 hour minimum, 15-minute increments, clock starts on-site) even when the customer raised load timing herself: 'it takes them a while to load up.'
top_strength: Garrison handled bad news well and then out-problem-solved it. When he discovered both Friday and Saturday had booked out overnight he owned it cleanly — 'I really do apologize, it looks like I've got a little bit of bad news here for you' — then immediately offered concrete alternatives (tomorrow, or Monday the 31st) with a real arrival window rather than a vague 'let me check.' The standout moment was unprompted: hearing that she was waiting on keys, he volunteered that the crew 'can kind of work autonomously,' so she could leave during the load, grab the key, and be ready at the destination. She reciprocated — 'That's true, that's true' — and stayed positive right through the goodbye despite having just lost her preferred dates.
coaching_note: Garrison, the single highest-leverage fix is asking for the booking on the call you already have. You found a live 8:30 AM slot for tomorrow, she told you she gets keys tomorrow, and you handed her the reason it could work — then let her hang up with nothing held. That sentence should have been: 'Sylvia, I've got one truck and two guys available tomorrow at 8:30, and there's no deposit to hold it — let me put your name on it right now, and if the keys fall through we can move it at no cost.' You had already watched Friday and Saturday disappear overnight; that is exactly the urgency to name out loud. Second priority: the piano. She told you the heaviest thing in the house is a piano and you said 'perfect, perfect' and moved on — that is where you explain the specialty handling, the crew and time implication, and our No Worries coverage up to $2,000, which is also the moment that earns trust with a repeat customer. Third, this call was a gift-wrapped Save Your Ass opening: she was already hauling garden items herself, so 'anything you can consolidate or take a carload of before we arrive shortens the move and lowers your bill — kids' toys, loose drawer items, photos off the walls. Does that make sense?' would have cost you thirty seconds and protected your estimate accuracy. Last, tighten the plumbing: use her name, pin the actual box count instead of accepting 'maybe six,' and say the word 'email' so she isn't sitting by the phone waiting for a callback that isn't coming.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently warm and affirming ('Oh, no worries at all,' 'that is a fantastic question,' 'I really do apologize'), and the unprompted key-pickup workaround built genuine rapport — held back from a 5 by heavy filler and repetition and by never once using the customer's name.
